newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany mulling amnesty for tax evaders-newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Germany mulling amnesty for tax evaders-newspaper.

text.p: Tax experts in Germany's ruling coalition are considering an amnesty for tax evaders in a bid to repatriate about 500 billion marks ($280.9 billion) invested offshore, a newspaper reported on Sunday.

Under the plan, investors would be charged a "settlement tax" of 20-25 percent tax on funds they bring back to Germany in return for exemption from prosecution, Gisela Frick, member of the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), was quoted as telling Bild am Sonntag newspaper.
The inflow would boost domestic investment and help Germany create much-needed jobs, Frick said.
Banks estimate that some 500 billion marks have been invested outside Germany, mainly in Luxembourg, since the beginning of 1994 to circumvent a 30 percent withholding tax on interest income.
"I am well aware that the amnesty is morally dubious -- we are talking about tax evasion after all," said Frick.
"But as we urgently need investment, such a measure would be justifiable, particularly as most tax refugees are leaving their money abroad due to the threat of legal action in Germany," she said.
The FDP is junior partner in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative-led coalition.
Several major German banks have had offices searched by tax authorities in recent years amid allegations that they have helped customers dodge tax.
Investing money abroad to avoid paying the withholding tax is not illegal but failing to report interest income to fiscal authorities in Germany is against the law. ($ = 1.78 German Marks)
